Historical model biases in monthly high temperature anomalies indicate under-estimation of future temperature extremes

Lei Duan, Lyssa M. Freese, Govindasamy Bala, and Ken Caldeira · Communications Earth & Environment 6, 604 · 2025

Key finding. CMIP6 models have underestimated 22-year-average monthly high-temperature anomalies by 2-3% and 22-year maximum anomalies by 11-12%; if those historical biases carry forward, average 2100 extreme high temperatures in some regions and months could exceed current projections by 3 K, and by more than 5 K in the most extreme cases.

What question did this research address?

The damage done by a heat extreme depends both on the mean climate state and on how far an individual month departs from that mean. Climate model evaluation has concentrated on the mean state; how well models reproduce the anomalies has been far less explored.

This paper asked how skilfully the models participating in the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) reproduce monthly high-temperature anomalies relative to monthly means, and what their historical errors imply for projected extremes.

What did we find?

Globally, the models underestimated 22-year-average monthly high-temperature anomalies by 2-3%, and underestimated 22-year maximum anomalies by 11-12%. The error is substantially larger for the extremes than for the average.

The biases are persistent rather than transient. Both positive and negative biases remain largely unchanged, regionally and seasonally, across the two historical periods examined — 1980 to 2001 and 2002 to 2023 — which is what justifies projecting them forward.

The models project that as the planet warms, high-temperature anomalies will grow in subtropical regions and shrink in high latitudes, so the anomaly component of an extreme is not simply a fixed offset added to a rising mean.

Carrying the historical biases forward implies that average 2100 extreme high temperatures in some regions and months could be about 3 K higher than currently projected, and more than 5 K higher in the most extreme cases.

Why does it matter?

Impacts from heat are driven by the extremes, not the averages, and a bias that is modest in the mean becomes large in the tail. An 11-12% underestimate of maximum anomalies translates into whole degrees of additional projected extreme heat.

Because the biases are stable across decades and identifiable by region and season, they can be corrected for rather than merely acknowledged — which makes this a usable adjustment to projections rather than only a caution about them.

Citation, data, and code

Lei Duan, Lyssa M. Freese, Govindasamy Bala, and Ken Caldeira (2025). Historical model biases in monthly high temperature anomalies indicate under-estimation of future temperature extremes. Communications Earth & Environment 6, 604.
